specAnchors.text: know that magnets repel and attract other magnets and attract magnetic substances
describe the properties of magnetically hard and soft materials

primer.text: Every magnet obeys one law — opposite poles attract, like poles repel — and the strongest pull sits at the poles. This note separates true magnets from merely magnetic materials, explains why repulsion is the only certain test, and splits the magnetic family into hard keepers and soft losers.

modules.title: The law of magnetism and the poles
modules.opening: Every magnet speaks one law: opposite poles attract, like poles repel — and attraction alone never proves a magnet, because magnets also pull unmagnetised magnetic substances towards them. The poles, where the pull is strongest, are where the law does its loudest talking.
keyPoints: The law of magnetism: opposite poles attract, like poles repel.
Magnetic forces are strongest at the poles of a magnet.
A magnet attracts magnetic substances as well as opposite poles, so attraction is not proof of magnetism.
Repulsion is the only certain test that an object is itself a magnet.
A suspended magnet settles with one pole pointing north — the north-seeking pole.

low.restatement: Bring two bar magnets end to end: two north poles push apart, a north and a south pull together, and either pole grabs an iron pin. The pulling and pushing is strongest at the very ends.
low.analogy: Think of two crowds where matching team shirts shove each other apart but opposite shirts hug — and everyone hugs bystanders carrying the team scarf.
low.examPointer: If a question asks for the certain test, answer repulsion — attraction only shows at least one object is magnetic, not that both are magnets.

medium.restatement: The law constrains every pole-pair interaction: force is attractive between unlike poles and repulsive between like poles, and it acts along the line joining the poles with maximum magnitude where the pole concentration is greatest. Because an unmagnetised magnetic material is attracted to either pole, only a repulsive outcome rules out mere induced magnetism.
medium.analogy: Two magnets behave like a room of people with strict handshake rules: rivals (alike) back away, friends (opposite) step in — and anyone neutral drifts towards whoever reaches out first.
medium.examPointer: Quote the law in full, then separate the two cases explicitly: magnet-to-magnet (attract or repel) versus magnet-to-substance (attract only). Examiners award the distinction.

modules.title: Magnetic materials, hard and soft
modules.opening: Magnetic substances — iron, steel, cobalt, nickel and some alloys — are the only materials a magnet can grab. Among them the hard/soft split decides careers: hard magnets keep their magnetism for good, while soft materials gain and lose it instantly, which is exactly what an electromagnet core needs.
keyPoints: Magnetic substances include iron, steel, cobalt and nickel; non-metals such as plastic and copper are non-magnetic.
Magnetically hard materials, like steel, keep their magnetism once magnetised — they make permanent magnets.
Magnetically soft materials, like pure iron, lose their magnetism easily — they make temporary magnets and electromagnet cores.
Magnetism is induced in a magnetic material when it is placed in a magnetic field.
A steel pin near an electromagnet is attracted the moment the current flows and released when it stops.

low.restatement: Some metals feel the pull of a magnet: iron, steel, cobalt, nickel. Steel holds its magnetism and becomes a permanent magnet; pure iron lets it go easily and works best inside electromagnets.
low.analogy: Hard materials are like a whiteboard marker that will not wipe off; soft materials wipe clean the moment the magnet is taken away.
low.examPointer: Name the four magnetic elements and match hard-with-steel and soft-with-iron explicitly — the pairing earns the mark.

medium.restatement: The classification turns on retention: hard magnetic materials have domains that lock into alignment, so magnetisation persists after the field is removed; soft materials realign freely, magnetising and demagnetising with the field. Induction is the field's ability to align an unmagnetised magnetic material's domains so the material itself gains poles — always with attraction as the outcome.
medium.analogy: A hard magnet is a comb that keeps its aligned teeth; a soft material is a comb whose teeth straighten out the instant you put it down.
medium.examPointer: For explain marks, tie the electromagnet-core choice to easy loss of magnetism when the current switches off — quoting 'soft iron core' alone is only half the answer.

glossary.definition: Opposite magnetic poles attract; like magnetic poles repel.
The region of a magnet where the magnetic force is strongest.
Magnetism created in a magnetic material while it sits in a magnetic field.
Describes a material that loses its induced magnetism as soon as the field is removed.
